source_acquisition.search_note: reports/tables/visual_source_inventory.csv listed ZinYY/Awesome-Parallel-Decoding as an automatic candidate; corpus/visual_sources/iclr-2026-dc06dcfe9933/ is empty. Read-only gh repo view and gh api recursive tree verified a parallel-decoding survey whose README has the exact paper title and arXiv link https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.15898, but its Code field is empty and its tree contains only README.md and asset/imgs/Parallel_Decoding_Logo.jpg. No plot*, figure*, visual*, table*, .tex, .tikz, .pgf, .svg, or notebook is present. gh exact-title code search and exact-title/method/ID repository searches returned no results. The PDF itself has no author code/project URL; therefore no candidate is recorded as a visual source.

paper_style.palette_strategy: Figures 1, 4 and 5 reuse Matplotlib-like tab colors, but k is color-coded in Figures 1/4 while n is color-coded in Figure 5. Figures 2/3 use a zero-centered RdBu-like diverging map. Tables are primarily black text with bold winners and red lower-bound/OOM values in Tables 1/3.
paper_style.vector_raster_mix: All five figures are embedded raster images with soft masks: Figure 1 has two 2250×1350 images, Figures 2/3 one 1783×1078 or 1800×1500 image each, Figure 4 four 2250×1350 images, and Figure 5 four 1800×2100 images. Table text/rules and captions are vector PDF objects; pdffonts shows Nimbus Roman/Computer Modern families.
paper_style.style_consistency: The PDF prose and tables use a stable embedded Nimbus Roman/Computer Modern system with roughly 8.7 pt table text, while the raster plots use DejaVu Sans appearance. Figure 2/3 are readable double-column images; Figure 1/4/5 contain many reduced panels and visibly smaller labels/legends, so figure typography is not consistent across objects.

figures.label: Figure 1

caption.text: Figure 1: Optimal acceptance rates from n i.i.d drafts with top-k sampling with n with target/draft pairs of Gemma-2 27B/2B and Llama-3 70/8B. Increasing k improves acceptance rate significantly up to k = 1000, and increasing n also results in steady increase in optimal acceptance.

color.semantic_mapping: Gemma panel: blue=k=10, orange=100, green=1000, red=10000, purple=100000, brown=256000; Llama panel uses brown for k=128256.

plot_grammar.legend_placement: lower right in each panel; repeated rather than shared

encodings.x: n (number of draft tokens), categorical/equally spaced values 1–10
encodings.color: top-k draft sampling; six tab colors map k=10,100,1000,10000,100000 and the model vocabulary size
encodings.shape: filled circular point markers for every series
encodings.line: solid connecting line for each k series
encodings.facet: two horizontal panels: Gemma-2 27B/2B and Llama-3 70B/8B
encodings.text: panel titles, axis labels, ticks, and per-panel legend; no direct point labels

figures.data_and_statistics: Point optimal-acceptance values over n=1…10 and six top-k settings per model. No sample count, dataset split, repetition/seed, denominator, or uncertainty is encoded; high-k curves overlap. The result trend is k=10 lowest, largest gains through k=1000, diminishing gains after k=10000, and continued n gains at larger k.
figures.evidence_relation: PDF p.8 §7.1 defines Gemma-2/Llama-3 pairs and n,k sweep; p.9 Figure 1 is the headline acceptance comparison. The adjacent p.9 paragraph sends the greedy comparison to Appendix O Figures 2–3; the object does not report solver time or multi-step latency.
design_strengths: Matched y-scale and aligned panels make the two model pairs directly comparable.
Circular marks preserve the discrete n observations while lines expose the trend.
Caption names the k≈1000 gain region and the n direction.
design_weaknesses: The two 2250×1350 raster panels are each reduced to about 198×119 pt, making plot labels and legends roughly 3–5.5 pt on the page.
All series use the same marker and line style, so color is the only k cue; high-k curves overlap and grayscale is unsafe.
No uncertainty, repetition, or vocabulary-size note is shown in the figure.
figures.reusable_pattern: Use matched dual-model line panels for a discrete n sweep with a common y scale; add marker/line-style redundancy, a shared legend, and uncertainty when reusing.

figures.label: Figure 2

caption.text: Figure 2: Comparison of i.i.d. versus greedy acceptance rates for Gemma-2 27B/2B across various choices of n and top-k sampling of the draft.

color.semantic_mapping: i.i.d. minus greedy acceptance: positive differences are blue, zero is near white, negative differences are orange/red.

encodings.x: n (number of draft tokens), categorical columns 2–10
encodings.y: k (top-k sampling of draft), categorical rows 10,100,1000,10000,100000,256000 shown equally spaced
encodings.color: continuous zero-centered difference i.i.d. optimal acceptance minus greedy optimal acceptance, colorbar about −0.015…+0.015
encodings.text: title, axis labels/ticks, and numeric colorbar ticks; no cell-value labels

figures.data_and_statistics: A 9×6 grid of Gemma-2 i.i.d.-minus-greedy optimal-acceptance differences. k=10 cells are mostly negative; k≥100 cells are mostly positive and high-k cells are dark blue. No absolute acceptance, prompt denominator, repeat/seed, or uncertainty is shown.
figures.evidence_relation: Appendix O p.28–29 expands the p.9 Figure 1 greedy comparison; Figure 2 resolves the aggregate claim by n×k condition for Gemma-2. It is an ablation/mechanism slice, not a runtime or multi-step result.
design_strengths: A zero-centered diverging map makes the sign of the i.i.d. advantage immediately visible.
The dense matrix exposes n×k interaction more compactly than many curves.
The full Gemma vocabulary endpoint k=256000 remains in the same map.
design_weaknesses: Unequal numeric k values are placed at equal vertical distances, which can imply a false linear spacing.
The key difference direction is absent from the caption and cell values are not printed.
Color is the sole encoding; light cells and small differences have no grayscale or texture redundancy.
figures.reusable_pattern: Use a fixed zero-centered n×k difference heatmap for ablation; label the difference direction and scale the k axis numerically or explicitly mark it categorical.

figures.label: Figure 3

caption.text: Figure 3: Comparison of i.i.d. versus greedy acceptance rates for Llama-3 70B/8B across various choices of n and top-k sampling of the draft.

color.semantic_mapping: i.i.d. minus greedy acceptance: positive differences are blue, zero is near white, negative differences are orange/red.

encodings.x: n (number of draft tokens), categorical columns 2–10
encodings.y: k (top-k sampling of draft), categorical rows 10,100,1000,10000,100000,128256 shown equally spaced
encodings.color: continuous zero-centered difference i.i.d. optimal acceptance minus greedy optimal acceptance, colorbar about −0.015…+0.015
encodings.text: title, axis labels/ticks, and numeric colorbar ticks; no cell-value labels

figures.data_and_statistics: A 9×6 grid of Llama-3 i.i.d.-minus-greedy optimal-acceptance differences. k=10 is negative, k≥100 is mostly positive, and the appendix text notes the i.i.d. advantage can decrease with n at high k. No absolute acceptance, prompt denominator, repeat/seed, or uncertainty is shown.
figures.evidence_relation: Appendix O p.28–29 pairs Figure 3 with Figure 2 to specialize the p.9 greedy comparison to Llama-3; the surrounding text states the high-k advantage weakens with n. It does not establish solver cost.
design_strengths: The Figure 2-compatible layout and colorbar make cross-model comparison straightforward.
The matrix presents a broad n×k sweep in one object.
Zero-centered colors preserve positive versus negative direction.
design_weaknesses: The Llama vocabulary endpoint k=128256 is equally spaced with much smaller k values.
Caption does not state that the cell is i.i.d. minus greedy.
No cell values, denominator, or uncertainty are available for close-to-zero cells.
figures.reusable_pattern: Keep coordinate geometry and color limits identical across paired model heatmaps, while adding an explicit difference legend, numeric labels, and scale note.

figures.label: Figure 4

caption.text: Figure 4: Optimal acceptance rates from n i.i.d drafts with top-k sampling with n with the target/draft pair Gemma-2 27B/2B, for various target temperature settings (0.2, 0.4, 0.6, 0.8). Until temperature 0.8, increasing k past 10 results in little acceptance gains for reasonable values of n.

color.semantic_mapping: Each target-temperature panel maps blue/orange/green/red/purple/brown to k=10,100,1000,10000,100000,256000.

plot_grammar.legend_placement: lower right in every panel; repeated rather than shared

encodings.x: n (number of draft tokens), categorical/equally spaced values 1–10
encodings.color: six top-k draft settings, same tab palette as Figure 1
encodings.text: panel titles, axes, ticks, and repeated six-item legends; no direct labels

figures.data_and_statistics: Four panels report point optimal acceptance over n=1…10 for six k values on Gemma-2 27B/2B. At temperatures 0.2 and 0.4 k=10 is near the top; at 0.8 k=10 trails as n grows. No sample count, repeat/seed, dataset facet, denominator, or uncertainty is shown.
figures.evidence_relation: Appendix Q p.30 extends the p.10 §7.3 temperature analysis and tests whether Figure 1’s k effect is temperature-dependent. Figure 4 is acceptance robustness/ablation; Figure 5 on p.31 separately covers global-resolution cost and failure.
design_strengths: A fixed y range and repeated k colors make temperature regimes easy to compare.
The 2×2 facet separates target-temperature conditions without changing the acceptance estimand.
The caption gives the temperature set and an overall k conclusion.
design_weaknesses: Four repeated legends consume space and shrink each 2250×1350 raster panel to roughly 190×114 pt.
Overlapping high-k curves and color-only encoding make small differences hard to trace.
The caption’s “reasonable values of n” is undefined and no repeated-run uncertainty is shown.
figures.reusable_pattern: Use fixed-scale parameter facets for a regime-change question; use one shared legend and redundant markers/linestyles to recover space and accessibility.

figures.label: Figure 5

caption.text: Figure 5: Solve times and failure rates of global resolution with τ = 10⁻⁴ (Gemma-2 27B/2B) for choices of k ∈ {10, 100, 1000, 10000} and n ∈ {2, 3, 4, 5}, plotted over increasing temperature.

color.semantic_mapping: Within each k block, blue/orange/green/red map to n=2,3,4,5; n=5 appears only for k=10.

plot_grammar.legend_placement: upper left in each lower failure-rate panel; repeated per block

encodings.y: Top subpanel: solve time in ms/token; bottom subpanel: failure rate in percent, both linear with block-specific ranges
encodings.facet: four k blocks (10,100,1000,10000), each paired as solve-time above failure-rate below
encodings.text: block titles, metric axes, ticks, and n legends; no direct labels

figures.data_and_statistics: Global resolution τ=10⁻⁴ on Gemma-2 27B/2B. Each k block plots solve time and failure rate over target temperature; k=10 has n=2–5 and other blocks n=2–4. The top y range is about 0–700 for k=10 and about 0–250/275 for the other blocks; the lower ranges also differ. Failure rate is a reported outcome, not uncertainty; no denominator, seed, or interval is shown.
figures.evidence_relation: Appendix Q p.31 Figure 5 extends Figure 4’s temperature robustness to global-resolution operational cost and failure. The p.10 §7.3 text invokes it for the low-temperature success/latency boundary; Appendix R later uses the solver in SpecTr.
design_strengths: Paired cost and failure panels share temperature as the horizontal variable, exposing an operational trade-off.
The n legend retains the special n=5 condition for k=10.
The separate solve-time and failure plots avoid falsely treating failure as an uncertainty band.
design_weaknesses: Eight axes and four repeated legends are dense; the 1800×2100 raster blocks render at only about 3–5.5 pt labels on the page.
Block-specific y ranges make cross-k height comparisons unsafe without reading ticks.
Color is the only n cue, and the caption omits the key low-temperature applicability conclusion.
figures.reusable_pattern: Pair cost and failure panels for each operating condition on a shared x variable; reuse with unified or explicitly annotated y scales, failure denominators, and a caption-level boundary statement.

tables.label: Table 1

caption.text: Table 1: Average Llama-3 solve times (ms/token) over k, n, for the five i.i.d. OTLP solvers. General LP and max-flow are baselines, and optimized max-flow and global resolution (τ = 10⁻³, 10⁻⁴) are ours. Lower numbers are better. Red numbers are lower bounds from small scale tests due to excessive runtime. Global resolution can be 10,000+ times faster than others. Global resolution deviates from the target distribution by at most 15τ in L1 distance, and from optimal acceptance by at most 10τ. We include success rates for global resolution as it can terminate early sometimes.

tables.uncertainty: No SD/SE/interval is shown. Parenthetical percentages are global-resolution success rates, not uncertainty; red 4000+/400000+ entries are lower bounds from small-scale tests and OOM is a failure state.
tables.data_and_statistics: Average Llama-3 solve times in ms/token for five i.i.d. OTLP solvers over seven (k,n) settings. Rows are (10,2): 4.07/2.45/2.51/5.27 (98%)/7.62 (93%); (10,3): 30.14/3.80/3.88/17.35 (98%)/23.95 (87%); (10,4): 4000+/74.21/74.37/40.30 (97%)/54.84 (86%); (10,5): 400000+/10000+/10000+/70.75 (96%)/94.79 (85%); (100,2): 4000+/72.28/63.03/23.92 (38%)/25.47 (23%); (100,3): 400000+/200000+/200000+/30.52 (23%)/38.44 (14%); (1000,2): OOM/400000+/400000+/34.94 (31%)/47.46 (15%), ordered General LP, Max-Flow, Opt. Max-Flow, G.R. τ=10⁻³, G.R. τ=10⁻⁴. Appendix M p.28 states 40 random prompts per dataset and CPU-only solver runs; only settings with at least one of the first three solvers under ten minutes/token are included.
tables.evidence_relation: p.9 §7.2 connects this table to Section 5.2/5.3 max-flow and Section 6 global resolution. It is the runtime/success counterpart to Figure 1’s acceptance headline and supplies the budget-selection inputs summarized by Table 2 on p.10.
design_strengths: One (k,n) row aligns all five methods for direct solver comparison.
Bold fastest entries and red lower bounds/OOM preserve both winner and infeasibility cues.
Caption defines units, lower-bound semantics, success rates, and approximation-error interpretation.
design_weaknesses: No prompt count, dispersion, seed, or hardware condition appears in the table itself.
Runtime and success rate share a cell, preventing independent sorting and making failure cost secondary.
Red lower bounds and OOM are visually grouped even though they are different states.
tables.reusable_pattern: Use setting rows × solver columns with bold row winners and a separate text cue for lower-bound/failure states; split runtime, success count, and failure state when the table is used operationally.

tables.label: Table 2

caption.text: Table 2: Best acceptance rates for baseline solvers (general LP) and ours (max-flow, optimized max-flow, global resolution with τ = 10⁻³, 10⁻⁴) on Llama-3 and Gemma-2 under average solve time limits of 10 and 100 ms/token. Optimized max-flow numbers are the same as max-flow.

tables.uncertainty: No variability or uncertainty is shown. Each value is the best aggregate acceptance found under an average runtime limit; winning (k,n) and failure counts are not included.
tables.data_and_statistics: Two runtime limits (10 and 100 ms/tok) × two model groups. Llama-3 values are 82.53/83.94/85.65/85.10% at 10 and 83.94/89.01/90.04/89.46% at 100; Gemma-2 values are 79.03/80.69/81.90/81.35% at 10 and 80.69/85.83/86.60/86.07% at 100, ordered Gen. LP, M.F., G.R. τ=10⁻³, G.R. τ=10⁻⁴. Optimized max-flow equals M.F. and is not a separate column.
tables.evidence_relation: p.9–10 §7.2 describes filtering by aggregate average runtime and fallback when global resolution fails; Table 2 converts Table 1’s speed measurements into a time-budget acceptance decision surface for both model pairs.
design_strengths: Two-level model/method header keeps both target models in one decision table.
Two-decimal percentages and within-group bold winners are highly scannable.
Runtime limits are explicit in the left stub and caption.
design_weaknesses: Best (k,n) configurations are absent, so the headline cannot be reproduced from the table alone.
Optimized max-flow is explained as equal to M.F. only in prose/caption, not in the header.
Average aggregation, failure handling, denominator, and repetition are not visible.
tables.reusable_pattern: Organize a resource-budget decision surface as limit × model group × method, retain group winners, and add the winning configuration plus failure/replicate fields.

tables.label: Table 3

caption.text: Table 3: Average Gemma-2 solve times (ms/token) over k, n, for the five i.i.d. OTLP solvers. General LP and max-flow are baselines, and optimized max-flow and global resolution (τ = 10⁻³, 10⁻⁴) are ours. Lower numbers are better. Red numbers are lower bounds from small scale tests due to excessive runtime. Global resolution can be 10,000+ times faster than others. Global resolution deviates from the target distribution by at most 15τ in L1 distance, and from optimal acceptance by at most 10τ. We include success rates for global resolution as it can terminate early sometimes.

tables.uncertainty: No SD/SE/interval is shown. Parenthetical percentages are global-resolution success rates; red lower bounds and OOM denote runtime/failure states.
tables.evidence_relation: Appendix P p.30 is the Gemma-2 companion to main Table 1; its matched columns expose model-specific runtime and success-rate differences while preserving the same global-resolution approximation claims.
design_strengths: The table is structurally isomorphic to Table 1, enabling model comparison without remapping columns.
Success rates remain visible beside runtime, and bold/red cues retain winner and infeasibility semantics.
Caption repeats the approximation and unit definitions needed to read the table alone.
design_weaknesses: Prompt denominator, dispersion, seeds, hardware, and successful-run counts are absent.
Red lower bounds and OOM are combined into one visual class, and success rate remains embedded in runtime cells.
Compressed headers require the caption to decode τ and method abbreviations.
tables.reusable_pattern: Use an exactly matched companion solver table for a second model; keep column semantics stable and separate time, success count, and failure status for reuse.

tables.label: Table 4

caption.text: Table 4: Block efficiency (number of decoded tokens per call to target model) in and walltime speedup (over vanilla autoregressive decoding) for SpecTr with global resolution under different values of K (number of i.i.d. paths). Experiments are run on Gemma-27B/2B with L = 8.

tables.uncertainty: No uncertainty, repetitions, raw walltime, or failure count is shown; all entries are point estimates.
tables.data_and_statistics: SpecTr on Gemma-27B/2B with target temperature 1.0, draft top-k=100, block length L=8. K=2,3,4 give block efficiency 2.23,2.54,2.65 tokens/M_p call and walltime speedup 1.84,1.89,1.98 relative to vanilla autoregressive decoding. Global-resolution failures fall back to p-sampling as described in Appendix R p.32.
tables.evidence_relation: Appendix R p.32 connects the single-step solver to end-to-end SpecTr latency; the p.10 §7.4 text cites the table for the nearly 2× walltime claim while the following paragraph qualifies it as conservative and situational.
design_strengths: A compact three-row K sweep keeps both efficiency estimands together.
Metric units and relative baseline are visible in the header and caption.
The narrow single-column table remains readable and black-and-white safe.
design_weaknesses: No baseline numeric column, error/repetition summary, or failure rate is available.
Readers need surrounding prose to discover fallback behavior and interpret “conservative”.
The caption has the printed grammatical fragment “in and walltime speedup”.
tables.reusable_pattern: Pair per-call efficiency with end-to-end speedup in a small parameter table, and add fallback/failure and replicate fields when the metric is operational.

tables.label: Table 5

caption.text: Table 5: Extending global resolution to three non-i.i.d. drafting regimes. Yes means the extension is immediate; Possible means it requires some work; No means there is a major obstacle.

tables.uncertainty: Qualitative Yes/Possible/No labels are not probabilities or measured uncertainty. “Possible” has an intentionally broad unresolved-work scope.
tables.data_and_statistics: Three drafting regimes × three global-resolution steps: sampling without replacement → Yes/Yes/Possible; n=2 independent and distinct → Yes/Possible/Possible; n≥3 independent and distinct → No/No/Possible. Step 1 is H* computation, Step 2 outer residuals, and Step 3 convex minimization, as explained in Appendix S p.33–34.
tables.evidence_relation: Appendix S p.33 presents the tractability matrix and then maps each cell to Appendices C/D/G/H/I/J and Section 6. It is the explicit limitation boundary for extending the method, not an experimental result.
design_strengths: A small regime × pipeline-step matrix makes the extension boundary visible in one glance.
The caption defines all three qualitative labels without relying on color.
Black-and-white rules and text remain robust for print.
design_weaknesses: “Possible” does not distinguish engineering effort from a theoretical bottleneck.
Long regime labels and minimal table width leave no room for complexity or evidence pointers.
The concrete O(V^5 log V) obstacle and source appendices appear only in following prose.
tables.reusable_pattern: Use an uncolored extension-regime × pipeline-step matrix with finite label definitions; add evidence/complexity pointers so qualitative cells cannot be mistaken for validated performance.

cross_object_system.visual_narrative: Main text moves from Figure 1 acceptance-versus-(n,k) headline to Table 1 solver runtime/success and Table 2 time-budget acceptance. Appendix O Figures 2/3 add greedy difference slices; Appendix P Table 3 mirrors runtime for Gemma; Appendix Q Figures 4/5 add temperature acceptance and cost/failure; Appendix R Table 4 connects to SpecTr walltime; Appendix S Table 5 closes with non-i.i.d. tractability.
cross_object_system.caption_system: Every object uses a regular-roman Figure/Table n: caption rather than a bold conclusion title. Tables 1/3 provide the richest unit, comparison, status, success-rate, and approximation definitions; Figures 2/3 and Tables 4/5 leave key findings to surrounding prose. Captions generally become self-contained with the object, but often omit difference direction, failure denominator, or winning configuration.
cross_object_system.table_header_system: Solver tables use (k,n) plus method columns; Table 2 adds two-level Llama-3/Gemma-2 model groups; Table 4 puts units in metric headers; Table 5 uses Drafting plus Step 1–3. Hierarchy is legible, but G.R./M.F. abbreviations depend on captions and optimized max-flow has no independent Table 2 column.
cross_object_system.method_result_ablation_link: Section 5 max-flow/optimized max-flow and Section 6 global resolution appear as method columns in Tables 1/3/2; Appendix O compares greedy, Q changes temperature, R tests SpecTr integration, and S decomposes non-i.i.d. extension. The method-to-result-to-boundary path is explicit but theory guarantees, success, and acceptance do not share one common visual encoding.
cross_object_system.main_appendix_link: p.9 Figure 1 explicitly points to Appendix O; p.10 §7.3 and §7.4 point to Q and R; Table 3 is the P counterpart of Table 1, and Figures 2/3 are the O difference views of Figure 1. Appendix objects reuse the main k/n colors and solver vocabulary while adding the detail omitted from the main page.
cross_object_system.typography_consistency: Tables share about 8.7 pt PDF-object Nimbus/Computer Modern text and consistent rules; all plot text is raster DejaVu Sans-like. Downscaled Figure 1/4/5 panels have about 3–5.5 pt page-visible labels, unlike the larger Figure 2/3 labels, creating a strong readability discontinuity.
cross_object_system.color_consistency: Tab colors are stable across line figures, with k semantics in Figures 1/4 and n semantics in Figure 5; heatmaps use a separate zero-centered red/blue semantic. Legends state the local mapping, but all curves lack marker/linestyle redundancy and color-only semantics are weak in grayscale.

most_reusable_patterns: Matched dual-model line panels for a discrete n sweep and common y-scale k trend.
Resource-limit × model-group × method table that turns runtime into an acceptance decision surface.
Paired solve-time/failure panels for temperature regimes plus an uncolored pipeline-step extension matrix.
failure_patterns: Downscaled raster panels in Figures 1/4/5 make typography and legends about 3–5.5 pt.
Curves, heatmap cells, and table statuses rely heavily on color/bold without redundant encoding.
Figures 2/3 place highly unequal k values at equal categorical distances.
Tables 1/3 combine runtime, lower bound/OOM, and success rate in cells; all experimental objects omit replication/denominator/uncertainty.
Figure 5 uses independent y ranges and its caption omits the main low-temperature applicability finding.
final_judgment.one_sentence_visual_strategy: The paper uses k/n color semantics, compact double-column multiples, zero-centered difference maps, and solver tables to connect high acceptance, low cost, and temperature/non-i.i.d. boundaries, trading away raster readability, accessibility redundancy, and replication detail for density.
